 ‘Our phones are being taken away,’ a White House reporter wrote from Air Force One as Trump left China
 After the president met with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, an Air Force One aide asked journalists to surrender the phones they’d used in China until they landed in the U.S.
 US President Donald Trump makes his way up to board Air Force One before departing from Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport following the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong, on November 19, 2026.
 Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images
 Christopher Wiggins 
 Nov 19, 2026
 Christopher Wiggins Christopher Wiggins is the politics and news editor at equalpride, where he leads and shapes coverage across The Advocate , Out , and Them . Based in Washington, D.C., he oversees national reporting on the White House, Congress, the Supreme Court, federal agencies, state governments, and the political forces shaping LGBTQ+ life in the United States.
 A GLAAD Media Award-winning journalist, Wiggins has reported extensively on federal policy, civil rights, elections, the courts, and the consequences of government action for LGBTQ+ people, with a particular focus on transgender communities. His work includes cover profiles for The Advocate’s print magazine featuring U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride of Delaware, CNN anchor-turned-independent journalist Don Lemon, former senior Centers for Disease Control and Prevention official Dr. Demetri Daskalakis, and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
 In addition to directing editorial strategy, Wiggins continues to report from Washington on the institutions, officials, and movements defining the national political landscape, including the second Trump administration.
 He can be reached at christopher.wiggins@equalpride.com and followed on Instagram and Bluesky . Whistleblowers and confidential sources may contact him securely on Signal at cwdc.98.

 Follow:
 Christopher Wiggins on X Just before 6 a.m. Thursday in Washington, D.C. , the news from Air Force One arrived in two sentences. President Donald Trump was leaving Shenzhen, China, after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Aurélia End, the Agence France-Presse correspondent covering the flight for the White House press pool, had one more detail for newsrooms as Trump headed home.
 “At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up. Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons,” End wrote, giving the local time in Shenzhen.
 Which reporters would have a working phone for the trip back to Washington depended on a choice they had made the day before.
 The explanation came from aboard the plane. In a midflight account that CNN’s Kaitlan Collins posted on X, CBS News correspondent Jennifer Jacobs said an Air Force One aide had asked journalists to place the phones they had used in China in a Faraday bag, a metal-lined pouch that blocks wireless signals. 
 The aide said the phones would be returned when the plane landed in the United States. Separately, the aide collected White House staffers’ temporary phones so they could be wiped or discarded, Jacobs reported.
 View on X Many reporters and photographers had brought temporary phones for the visit, leaving their everyday devices aboard Air Force One before landing in China on Wednesday. Once back on board, they could retrieve those devices and use them to file. Their colleagues who had carried their regular phones in Shenzhen faced the long flight home without a cellphone.
 The traveling pool serves as the eyes and ears of newsrooms that have no one aboard Air Force One. On Thursday, its members sent updates down to the minute, including when Trump’s motorcade reached the airport and what reporters could see from beneath the wing as he boarded. Jacqui Heinrich, a Fox News correspondent and president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, noted that reporters kept their phones when Trump left Beijing in May.
 Jacobs described the measure as a cybersecurity precaution. When NBC News correspondent Gabe Gutierrez reached Trump by phone and asked what had prompted it, the president did not identify a specific threat.
 View on X “Well, we want to be careful, and we didn’t want to have people have phones when they shouldn’t have phones, so we were very careful,” Trump said.
 The traveling press pool had already been aboard a presidential decoy flight once this year. In July, after a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, reporters flew out believing Trump was on their plane. The White House had said he was aboard. Weeks later, The Washington Post reported that Trump had secretly left on a different military jet after U.S. officials learned of a possible Iranian assassination plot. 
 The journalists and some White House staffers on the decoy flight had no idea the president had switched planes.
